memo_script:
So there's this little suffix that Tamil speakers stick onto almost everything — and once you hear it, you'll hear it everywhere.

It's -இட்டு. Or in fast speech, just -ட்டு. And it means the thing is *done*. Finished. Off you go.

வந்துட்டேன் — I've arrived, I'm here, done.
கழுவிட்டு வரேன் — let me wash up and I'll come, I'll be right there.
ஆயிட்டேன் — I'm ready, sorted, done.
விட்டுடு — just let it go, leave it, it's over.

Native speakers don't decide to add it. It just *falls out*. It's the sound of wrapping something up without making a big deal of it. Very Coimbatore — we don't linger on the transition, we just move.

The English cousin is 'I've gone and done it' — but we do it in one breath, not five words.

You already have seven deck items that live inside this pattern. Next time you see ட்டு at the end of something, you'll know exactly what it's doing.

You already used this one. At dinner, two weeks ago, you said 'Canada-la irukkom' — Canada-ல இருக்கோம். That ல at the end? That's the whole thing.

In Tamil, there's no separate word for 'in', 'at', or 'on'. You just stick ல onto the noun and you're done. வீட்ல — at home. போன்ல — on the phone. தமிழ்ல — in Tamil. கனடாவுல — in Canada. Same suffix, every time. The whole locative case, one sound.

Now here's the part I love. This suffix is so old, linguists trace it back over two thousand years — it shows up in Sangam poetry, same form, same job. The world changed, the word didn't. While English was still sorting out whether to say 'in' or 'at' or 'on' depending on context, Tamil had already decided: ல. Done.

And you'll hear it bent a little in Coimbatore. வீட்ல sometimes becomes வீட்லே — a tiny stretch, more feeling in it. Like you're really home. Same meaning, just warmer.

You're already saying it. You just didn't know what you were saying.

body: 🎙️ the word that means 'it happened, move on' — ஆச்சு. one ending, a hundred situations. 60 sec.
memo_script:
ok so you know how in English you say 'it's done' or 'that happened' or 'time's up' — three different sentences for three different things?

Tamil does all of that with one ending: ஆச்சு.

யாரோ வந்தாங்க, சாப்பிட்டோம், போனோம் — and then: நேரம் ஆச்சு. time happened. it's time. we go.

Or the food's ready: சமைச்சாச்சு. the cooking became-done.

Or your maama is waving you off after the meal: ஆச்சு ஆச்சு — done done, enough, go sit.

The pattern: take any verb and push ச்சு onto the end. போ becomes போச்சு — it went, it's gone, that chapter closed. முடி becomes முடிஞ்சுச்சு — finished-happened.

The soul of it: ஆச்சு doesn't just report the past. it *closes* it. the thing landed. we move now.
